The app adds no claim of its own: each filter type points at its Exposure Index row where the Index has one. Do not retype: update from the guide.

types.label: Under-sink reverse osmosis
types.study: In a 2020 study of North Carolina homes, under-sink reverse-osmosis and two-stage filters removed nearly all PFAS tested.

types.label: Carbon pitcher, tap or under-sink carbon
types.study: In a 2020 study of North Carolina homes, pitcher, faucet and other carbon filters removed about 60–70% of long-chain and about 40% of short-chain PFAS.

types.label: Whole-house carbon
types.study: In a 2020 study of North Carolina homes, four of eight whole-house carbon systems raised PFAS levels.

types.label: No filter, or I don't know
types.study: On a public supply, ask your water utility what it has measured for PFAS, or ask it to test; this is the first step US EPA suggests. On a private well, test regularly with a lab certified for PFAS analysis (EPA methods 533 and 537.1).

steps.title: The label names PFAS reduction
steps.text: A filter can be certified to NSF/ANSI 53 for something else, such as lead, so the certification has to name PFAS reduction — and the type of PFAS you are trying to remove.

steps.title: The certifier's own listing
steps.text: Search the exact model number in the certifier's directory: the listing names PFOA and PFOS, or "Total PFAS". EPA lists five certification bodies: NSF · UL · WQA · CSA Group · IAPMO R&T.

steps.title: Keep it working
steps.text: Filters are only effective if they are maintained to the manufacturer's replacement interval. Put it in your calendar.

where: US certification standards and US EPA limits. Outside the United States, ask your water supplier what it measures and which certifications your national authority recognises.
